question_text: A developer must select a foundation model for a legal document summarisation service. Requirements are: minimal hallucinations, support for 100K-token context windows, and a cost under $0.002 per 1K tokens. Which evaluation approach is correct?

options.text: Choose the model with the highest parameter count — more parameters always mean better accuracy
Evaluate models using performance benchmarks on representative legal documents, context window capability analysis, and price-to-performance ratio comparison
Select the most recently released Bedrock model as it will always outperform older ones
Use SageMaker Autopilot to automatically select the best FM

explanation: Skill 1.2.1 prescribes performance benchmarks, capability analysis, and limitation evaluation for FM selection. For this scenario: benchmark hallucination rates on legal text, verify the model supports 100K-token contexts, and compare price-to-performance ratios. Parameter count alone does not predict domain-specific quality. Recency does not guarantee domain fit. SageMaker Autopilot is for traditional ML AutoML, not FM selection.
source_topic: FM selection, Amazon Bedrock model catalogue

question_text: A company wants its GenAI application to switch between Claude, Titan, and Llama models based on runtime cost and latency conditions without redeploying code. Which architecture supports this?

options.text: Hardcode model IDs in Lambda environment variables and redeploy when routing changes are needed
Store model routing configuration in AWS AppConfig; Lambda reads the configuration at invocation time
Query an RDS table for model preferences on every FM invocation
Use SageMaker Experiments to track which model performs best, then manually update the code

explanation: Skill 1.2.2 explicitly cites AWS AppConfig for flexible architecture patterns that enable dynamic model selection without code modifications. AppConfig supports real-time config updates with rollout controls and automatic rollback. Hardcoded Lambda environment variables require redeployment. RDS queries add latency and coupling to every FM call. SageMaker Experiments tracks results but doesn't provide runtime routing.
source_topic: AWS AppConfig, dynamic model routing, Lambda

question_text: An application deployed in us-east-1 requires a specific Claude model version that is only available in us-west-2. The team also needs the application to remain operational if one region degrades. Which Bedrock feature directly addresses both needs?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput in us-east-1
Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference
AWS Global Accelerator routing to a Bedrock endpoint
Amazon CloudFront caching Bedrock responses for multi-region delivery

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region Inference lets an application in one region invoke a model available only in another region, and can route to alternate regions for resilience — directly matching Skill 1.2.3. Provisioned Throughput provides reserved capacity within a single region and doesn't solve cross-region model availability. Global Accelerator optimises network routing but doesn't address FM model availability. CloudFront caches static content — not appropriate for dynamic FM invocations.

question_text: During a regional service degradation, calls to Amazon Bedrock time out and cascading failures bring down downstream services. Which architectural pattern prevents this?

options.text: Increase Lambda timeout to 15 minutes to allow Bedrock time to recover
Use AWS Step Functions to implement a circuit breaker — open the circuit after a failure threshold and return a cached or default response
Disable retry logic so additional requests do not pile up on the degraded service
Synchronously poll Bedrock in a while loop until it responds

explanation: Skill 1.2.3 explicitly names AWS Step Functions circuit breaker patterns for AI system resilience. When failure rate exceeds a threshold the circuit opens and callers receive a fallback immediately — preventing cascades. Increasing Lambda timeout merely delays failures without adding a fallback path. Disabling retries removes resilience without substituting a fallback. Synchronous polling wastes compute and fails just as hard.
source_topic: Circuit breaker, AWS Step Functions, Bedrock resilience

question_text: A company wants to customise a large FM for a specialised task using their proprietary data. GPU budget is limited and they cannot afford full fine-tuning. Which technique should they use?

options.text: Full fine-tuning of all model parameters
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)
Pre-training from scratch on domain data
Zero-shot prompting with the largest available model

explanation: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes most model parameters and injects small trainable low-rank matrices, dramatically cutting GPU memory and compute versus full fine-tuning. It is explicitly listed under Skill 1.2.4 as a parameter-efficient adaptation technique. Full fine-tuning trains all billions of parameters — very expensive. Pre-training from scratch is even more expensive. Zero-shot prompting doesn't update model weights at all.
source_topic: LoRA, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Bedrock custom models

question_text: A team has fine-tuned a domain-specific FM and needs to version it, promote it to production with a deployment pipeline, and roll back automatically if accuracy drops. Which set of AWS services best supports this? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry for model versioning and approval workflows
AWS CodeCommit to store model weights as Git LFS objects
Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints with automated deployment pipelines and rollback strategies
AWS Backup for scheduled model artefact snapshots
Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies to archive old model versions

explanation: Skill 1.2.4 cites SageMaker Model Registry for versioning and deploying customised models, and SageMaker AI endpoints with automated deployment pipelines and rollback strategies. CodeCommit/Git LFS is not suited to multi-gigabyte model artefacts. AWS Backup targets workload data/resources, not ML model lifecycle. S3 Lifecycle policies archive or delete objects — they provide no deployment or rollback capability.
source_topic: SageMaker Model Registry, SageMaker endpoints, model lifecycle

question_text: A company wants multiple application teams to access foundation models through a unified internal endpoint that enforces authentication, logs usage, and can route to different models without changing client code. Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Give each team direct IAM access to Bedrock with no abstraction layer
Deploy an Amazon API Gateway-backed Lambda function as a GenAI gateway that authenticates callers, routes to the appropriate model, and logs all invocations
Share a single IAM user credential among all teams for simplicity
Use Amazon CloudFront as a proxy in front of Bedrock

explanation: Skill 1.2.2 describes flexible architecture patterns that enable dynamic model selection — an API Gateway + Lambda GenAI gateway is the canonical pattern. It centralises auth (via Cognito/API key/IAM), enables per-team usage logging, and allows backend model routing changes without client code changes. Direct per-team IAM access scatters governance. Sharing an IAM user credential is a security anti-pattern. CloudFront is a CDN/edge proxy — not designed for dynamic FM routing and auth.
source_topic: GenAI gateway, API Gateway, Lambda, Bedrock

question_text: A production GenAI application requires guaranteed, consistent inference throughput for a custom fine-tuned model on Amazon Bedrock, regardless of other customers' usage. Which Bedrock feature provides this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference (pay-per-token with no guarantees)
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput — reserve model units (MUs) for dedicated capacity
Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoints with autoscaling
AWS Lambda reserved concurrency

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput lets you purchase Model Units (MUs) — dedicated capacity for a specific model — guaranteeing consistent throughput regardless of shared-service contention. This is referenced in Skill 2.2.1 as a deployment option for specific performance requirements. On-demand inference is subject to throttling. SageMaker endpoints are for non-Bedrock models. Lambda reserved concurrency governs Lambda invocations, not Bedrock model capacity.

question_text: Which statement about accessing foundation models through Amazon Bedrock is CORRECT?

options.text: Bedrock only offers Amazon's own Titan models
Bedrock provides access to FMs from multiple providers (Amazon, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, etc.) through a single unified API
You must negotiate a separate contract with each model provider before using Bedrock
Bedrock only supports text modality — no image or embedding models are available

explanation: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers foundation models from Amazon (Titan), Anthropic (Claude), Meta (Llama), Mistral, Cohere, AI21 Labs, and others through a single API surface. This is a core architectural advantage — model switching without multi-vendor contract management. Bedrock also offers embedding models (Amazon Titan Embeddings) and image generation models (Amazon Titan Image, Stability AI).

question_text: A developer builds a structured-output assistant that should stop generating immediately after it emits the closing tag </answer>. The output sometimes continues past this tag with extraneous text. Which inference parameter reliably fixes this?

options.text: Add a prompt instruction: 'Stop after </answer>'
Set the stop_sequences parameter to ["</answer>"] in the inference API call
Lower the temperature to 0 to make the model more deterministic
Reduce top_k to 1 to restrict the vocabulary

explanation: The stop_sequences inference parameter instructs the Bedrock server to halt token generation the instant the specified string is produced — a 100% reliable server-side brake. Prompt instructions (A) are advisory and the FM may ignore them, especially at higher creativity settings. Temperature (C) controls randomness, not stopping behaviour. top_k (D) limits vocabulary breadth, not where generation ends.
source_topic: Stop sequences, inference parameters, Amazon Bedrock

question_text: A financial institution processes 80,000 contract summaries nightly in a predictable 4-hour batch window and requires stable, consistent latency with no shared-queue delays. Which Bedrock pricing mode is most appropriate?

options.text: On-Demand — pay per token, no commitment
Provisioned Throughput — purchase Model Units for a committed term to guarantee dedicated capacity
EC2 Spot instances with a self-hosted open-source model
Lambda reserved concurrency with Bedrock on-demand

explanation: Bedrock Provisioned Throughput purchases dedicated Model Units for a 1-6 month commitment, guaranteeing stable latency with no shared-queue contention — ideal for large, predictable, high-volume batch workloads. On-Demand is pay-per-token but subject to throttling under shared load. Bedrock has no Spot pricing option. Lambda reserved concurrency governs Lambda invocations, not Bedrock model capacity.

question_text: A team is building a multimodal assistant on Amazon Bedrock that must process text, images, and video inputs. They need a cost-effective AWS-native model family that supports all three modalities. Which Amazon FM family is specifically designed for this?

options.text: Amazon Nova (Nova Pro / Nova Lite / Nova Micro) — AWS's latest multimodal model family
Amazon Titan Text Express — optimized for long text generation only
Amazon Titan Image Generator — image generation only
Amazon Lex — conversational AI for voice and text only

explanation: Amazon Nova is AWS's latest foundation model family, with Nova Pro and Nova Lite supporting text, image, and video inputs (multimodal), and Nova Micro optimized for text at lowest cost. Titan Text Express handles text only, Titan Image Generator generates images but does not accept video/text input for reasoning, and Lex is a conversational AI service — not a general FM.

topic: Reasoning models — cost vs accuracy trade-off
question_text: A developer is choosing between a standard FM and a reasoning-enabled FM for a complex multi-step financial analysis task on Amazon Bedrock. Which statement CORRECTLY describes the trade-off of enabling model reasoning?

options.text: Reasoning models apply chain-of-thought internally, yielding higher accuracy on complex tasks but at higher token cost and increased latency
Reasoning models are always cheaper because they use fewer tokens
Reasoning models disable the system prompt, so they cannot follow instructions
Reasoning models only work with image inputs, not text

explanation: Enabling reasoning on a foundation model activates chain-of-thought processing: the model breaks a complex task into internal reasoning steps before producing the final answer. This improves accuracy on complex problems but uses more tokens (thinking tokens + output tokens) and adds latency. Reasoning models do not reduce token usage, do not disable system prompts, and work with text inputs.

topic: Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings — input format
question_text: A developer is indexing product images and descriptions into a single vector index using Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1. How must image data be provided to this model's API?

options.text: As base64-encoded binary within a structured JSON request body
As a raw JPEG file uploaded to a dedicated image endpoint
As an S3 presigned URL passed directly in plain text
As a multipart/form-data POST with separate text and image parts

explanation: Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 requires image data to be base64-encoded and included inside a structured JSON request body alongside the text inputs. Raw file uploads, plain presigned URLs, and multipart form-data are not the accepted input format for this API.
source_topic: Amazon Titan Multimodal Embeddings, API input format
